newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German metal sector seeks wage system overhaul.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German metal sector seeks wage system overhaul.

text.p: Germany's huge metal and engineering sector, employing some four million workers in industries from car-making to electronics, on Wednesday began talks aimed at reforming the wage bargaining system that has served it from the 1950s.

Entering the talks, which are expected to develop into months of detailed negotiations, IG Metall, Germany's largest trade union, said that its priority would be to secure agreements allowing early retirment in the sector.
"This is an absolute priority," IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel told journalists before the first round of talks began in a hotel in Frankfurt.
"Young workers must be given a possibility of employment in the sector and old workers must be allowed to move into retirement under acceptable circumstances," he added.

Employers in the industry, which last year shed jobs at a rate of over 100,000 a month, however insisted that making wage contracts in the sector more flexible was necessary to bolster German firms' competitiveness against foreign rivals.
"Current sector-wide wage contracts are not workable (for many firms in the industry)," Werner Stumpfe, president of the Gesamtmetall employers federation said.

Union officials are hoping that talks will return to a model they have already proposed that would allow workers effectively to retire five years early while retaining their full pension entitlements.

Under the proposed model, 55-year-old workers would receive 85 percent of their full salary for the last 10 years of their working life. They would then work full-time for five years before being released at the age of 60.
Under the scheme, which IG Metall says has the support of the Bonn government, pension contributions would continue to be paid in full for the last 10 years.
A similar system is already being discussed at Europe's largest car-maker Volkswagen AG, IG Metall officials said earlier this week.

Employers in the industry are meanwhile seeking to have exemption clauses built in to collective wage agreements that would, for example, more easily allow companies to save costs by operating at reduced capacity when business was turning down.

IG Metall is against such clauses, but has indicated it would be ready to accept so-called "hardship" clauses currently used in east German contracts under which, under certain circumstances, firms are able to reduce wages for a limited period.
Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe said he did not expect overall agreement on the reforms before the end of the year.
It further remains to be seen whether the mood of the talks is in any way influenced by the bruising encounter between IG Metall and Gesamtmetall late last year on plans to cut sick pay entitlements.
Sick payments were ultimately left unchanged at 100 percent of salary after protests involving hundreds of thousands of metal and engineering workers.
